title: Africa 1 of 8 · North Africa
edition: Africa countries · Eight regional lessons · John · November 2026
intro: Welcome to Africa episode one of eight. First, I clear the chosen names for a fresh regional lesson.
We begin along the Mediterranean, from Morocco to Egypt, then locate Western Sahara on the Atlantic. There are five countries and one disputed territory in this episode.

states.name: Morocco
lines: Morocco occupies Africa’s northwestern corner, facing the Atlantic and the Mediterranean. The Strait of Gibraltar separates its northern coast from Spain. Algeria lies east.
The old city of Fez preserves schools, mosques, fountains and merchants’ buildings from its long history as a cultural centre. Its streets recall a city organised around learning and trade.
Picture the old streets of Fez at Africa’s northwestern gateway. Morocco has two sea fronts; Algeria stretches east along the Mediterranean.
states.transition: Let's bring Morocco and its neighbours into view.

states.name: Algeria
lines: Algeria lies east of Morocco and west of Tunisia and Libya. A Mediterranean coast tops a broad territory extending deep into the Sahara.
At Tassili n’Ajjer, prehistoric drawings and engravings record animals, people and changing environments. The rock art is a reminder that today’s desert has a much longer environmental history.
Think of a great rock-art gallery beneath a Mediterranean roof. Algeria reaches far south into the Sahara; it is much more than its coastal strip.

states.name: Tunisia
lines: Tunisia is the smaller Mediterranean country between Algeria and Libya. Its northern coast faces the central Mediterranean, with Sicily across the water.
Carthage developed into a powerful Mediterranean trading city before Rome destroyed it and later built a Roman city on the same site. One place preserves several layers of history.
Picture trading ships beside the small northern wedge. Tunisia fits between broad Algeria and Libya; do not move Carthage to the opposite side of the Mediterranean.

states.name: Libya
lines: Libya lies east of Tunisia and Algeria, west of Egypt, and north of Chad and Niger. Most of its territory extends inland from the Mediterranean into the Sahara.
The Roman emperor Septimius Severus was born at Leptis Magna, on this coast. He later enlarged the city, whose remains include a harbour, public buildings and a marketplace.
Remember an emperor’s home city on the Mediterranean above a vast desert. Libya is the broad coastal link between Tunisia and Egypt.
states.transition: Let's bring Libya and its neighbours into view.

states.name: Egypt
lines: Egypt anchors Africa’s northeastern corner, with Libya west and Sudan south. The Nile runs toward the Mediterranean; the Sinai Peninsula lies across the Suez Canal in Asia.
The pyramid fields around ancient Memphis include Giza, Saqqara and Dahshur. These monuments belong to a wider funerary landscape, rather than a single isolated pyramid.
Follow the Nile north to its delta and remember the pyramid landscape beside it. Keep Egypt at the Mediterranean and Red Sea meeting point.
states.transition: Let's bring Egypt and its neighbours into view.

states.name: Western Sahara
lines: Western Sahara is the Atlantic territory south of Morocco and north and west of Mauritania. GeoClick presents it as a separate map target.
The United Nations lists Western Sahara as a Non-Self-Governing Territory. Its status is unresolved, so this separate teaching stop does not treat a simplified map boundary as a political settlement.
Remember the disputed Atlantic strip below Morocco. We distinguish this territory from the fifty-four countries in our Africa coverage and do not infer control from the map.
states.transition: Let's bring Western Sahara and its neighbours into view.

recap: From west to east, follow Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya and Egypt. Remember Fez, Saharan rock art, Carthage, an emperor’s home city and the pyramid fields beside the Nile.

Western Sahara lies south of Morocco on the Atlantic. It is a separate disputed-territory stop, not an extra country in our fifty-four-country coverage. Map outlines do not settle status or show control.
